progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: Year 11 (n = c × V with V in litres; n = m / M; balanced equations and mole ratios). C02 (acid reactions and their products: acid + hydroxide → salt + water; acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide; balancing, including sulfuric acid with two hydroxides). C05 (strong and weak; ethanoic acid is weak and mostly un-ionised). C08 (only a small fraction of a weak acid is ionised; [H₃O⁺] is far below c). C07 (pH is −log[H₃O⁺]; strong acids give [H₃O⁺] = c). C06 (carbonate accepts protons; a diprotic acid gives two). Module 5: Le Chatelier's principle. Not assumed: titration apparatus and terms, primary standard, standardisation, concordance.
progression.startsWith: Use a known standard and an unknown solution. The video opens: The label on this white vinegar says five per cent acidity. How could you check how much ethanoic acid is really in it? A pH meter won't do it well.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why a pH reading gives a weak acid's concentration only very imprecisely, but a titration counts it; describing a titration with a standard solution, pipette, burette and indicator, and distinguishing the endpoint from the equivalence point; explaining why a titration counts all of a weak acid; stating what makes a primary standard and why sodium hydroxide is standardised; choosing concordant titres (within 0.10 mL) and averaging only those; calculating an unknown concentration in four steps (balanced equation and ratio, n = cV for the known, the ratio for the unknown, c = n/V) with 1 : 1 and 1 : 2 ratios, whichever solution is in the burette, to the right significant figures. No rinsing, meniscus, bubble or error-direction technique (chem-m6-p06), no indicator choice (chem-m6-c13), no curves (chem-m6-c14), no back titration or aliquot scale-up (chem-m6-c15, chem-m6-g03).
progression.nextLesson: doing a titration in the lab, with the technique that keeps it accurate (route chem-m6-p06).

teaching.task: A pH meter can't tell you accurately how much ethanoic acid is in a bottle of vinegar. How does a titration count every acid molecule, which titres can you trust, and how do the balanced equation and n = cV turn a titre into a concentration?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a pH meter gives the concentration of a weak acid only very imprecisely, because it senses only the small ionised fraction and working back through Ka magnifies the reading error; we need to count every acid molecule (1); (2) react it with a solution of exactly known concentration and measure how much is needed; apparatus and terms (2); (3) the equivalence point is reached when the amounts match the equation, and the endpoint shows it; hydroxide keeps removing hydronium, so the weak acid keeps ionising until all of it has reacted (3); (4) the known concentration must be trustworthy: primary standards; NaOH absorbs water and CO₂, so its solution is standardised (4); (5) a rough titre locates the endpoint; accurate titres must agree within 0.10 mL; average only those (5); (6) the balanced equation gives the ratio; moles of the known from n = cV (6); (7) the ratio gives moles of acid; divide by the aliquot volume; four significant figures; compare with the label (7); (8) the ratio is not always 1 : 1: carbonate takes two protons, so two HCl per Na₂CO₃ (8); (9) moles of carbonate, times two, divided by the titre volume: the unknown can be in the burette (9); memory aid (10); two attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); decision rule and handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: one limitation carries the video: a pH meter cannot tell you accurately how much ethanoic acid is in vinegar, because it senses only the small ionised fraction. A titration counts every acid molecule instead: hydroxide from a solution of exactly known concentration keeps removing hydronium, so the weak acid keeps ionising until all of it has reacted, and the endpoint shows when the amounts match the equation. Primary standards and concordant titres say which numbers to trust, and two worked examples (vinegar against sodium hydroxide, then hydrochloric acid in the burette against sodium carbonate, a two to one ratio) run the same mole bridge: known to moles, ratio, unknown. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: The label on this white vinegar says five per cent acidity. How could you check how much ethanoic acid is really in it? A pH meter won't do it well. Ethanoic acid is weak, so most of it stays as whole molecules, and the meter only senses the few that have ionised. You could work back through K a, but a reading of two point four could mean anything from about zero point seven to one point one moles per litre. You need a method that counts every acid molecule. That's a titration. So how does it work, and how do its numbers give a concentration?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A 25.00 mL aliquot of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, of unknown concentration was titrated with 0.1000 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution. The titres were 23.45 mL, 23.70 mL, 23.40 mL and 23.50 mL. Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid." New acid with a 1 : 2 ratio the student must write, and a non-concordant titre. Crossed mistake: "1 : 1, so c = 0.09380 mol/L" (the site's Step 3 error). (A2) "Two conical flasks each contain a 25.00 mL aliquot of an acid. Flask A contains 0.100 mol/L hydrochloric acid, HCl, and flask B contains 0.100 mol/L ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH. Each is titrated with 0.100 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution. Predict the volume of sodium hydroxide needed to reach the equivalence point in each flask. Explain your prediction, given that the two acids have different pH values." Tests the hook's idea on an unseen pair. Crossed mistake: "B needs less NaOH, because ethanoic acid is only partly ionised".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct practical investigations to analyse the concentration of an unknown acid or base by titration" this video starts from a known standard and an unknown solution and stops at the unknown's concentration from concordant titres and a balanced mole ratio. It teaches: why a pH reading gives the concentration of a weak acid such as ethanoic acid only very imprecisely (C05, C08 and C10 callbacks), and why a titration counts it; the idea of a titration (react the unknown with a solution of exactly known concentration until the amounts match the equation); the apparatus and terms (standard solution, pipette and aliquot, burette, titrant, titre, indicator, endpoint, equivalence point) at the level needed for the calculation; why a titration counts all of a weak acid (hydroxide removes hydronium, the equilibrium shifts right until every molecule has reacted; Module 5 Le Chatelier callback); what makes a primary standard and why sodium hydroxide is standardised first; rough and accurate titres and concordance (within 0.10 mL); the four-step calculation with a 1 : 1 ratio (vinegar) and a 1 : 2 ratio (sodium carbonate standardising hydrochloric acid, with the unknown in the burette); significant figures for the result. Not here: rinsing rules, meniscus reading, parallax, air bubbles, the rough-titration technique and error direction (chem-m6-p06, the next video, which owns practical conduct and error evaluation; see Open decisions); indicator choice and equivalence-point pH (chem-m6-c13); titration curves and conductivity graphs (chem-m6-c14); back titration and dilution or aliquot scale-up from a volumetric flask (chem-m6-c15 and chem-m6-g03; see Open decisions); percentage by mass with density (g03); polyprotic stages of tartaric or oxalic acid beyond the overall ratio.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout: H₃O⁺ teal token on pale blue water (C01); OH⁻ violet; whole ethanoic acid molecules amber-outlined (C05, C08); the known solution's values (standard, titrant) navy; the unknown's values amber; the ratio box teal; concordant titres ringed teal, the outlier crossed grey. Board layout (constant, C03, C07, C08 and C10): top-left the short task line; the left column holds the givens card during worked examples (grouped, units attached); the centre holds the titre table, the mole bridge or the working, one stage per line, earlier lines dimming; the apparatus plates sit small at the right only when they carry the explanation. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 20 Oct): `m6-burette-clamp-stand-v1.png` (inspected: retort stand, clamp and glass burette with a blue tap, no person or hand; scenes 2, 3, 5, the fill gauge drawn over its tube), `m6-volumetric-pipette-filler-v1.png` (inspected: bulb pipette with a red pipette filler, no hand; scene 2), `m6-conical-flask-v1.png` and `m6-white-tile-v1.png` (scene 2, under the burette tip), `m6-clip-phenolphthalein-colourless-v1.png` and `m6-clip-phenolphthalein-pink-v1.png` (inspected the pink one: conical flask of pale pink solution, no hand; scene 3, the endpoint swap), `m6-vinegar-bottle-v1.png` (hook and scenes 5 to 7, coded label "white vinegar: 5% acidity"), `m6-ph-meter-probe-beaker-v1.png` (hook, coded readout "2.4" in the beaker labelled "vinegar"), `m6-volumetric-flask-v1.png` (scene 4, the standard solution), `m6-indicator-methyl-orange-set-v1.png` (not used: indicator choice is chem-m6-c13; scene 8 names the indicator in a tag only). No new plates needed. No human figures.
